Externally gestated embryos of California ground squirrels develop within the uterus over a gestation period of 30 days [tg = 30 days], a relatively short duration for a rodent of this body size at a temperature of 35.6 °C [T = 35.6 °C]. This rapid embryogenesis, occurring at a maternal body temperature of 35.6 °C [T = 35.6 °C], allows females to deliver altricial neonates that are highly dependent on maternal care. The pups are born after a live birth event, and each newborn weighs approximately 7.8 grams [Wwb = approximately 7.8 grams], a value inferred from congeneric species such as Otospermophilus variegatus. This modest birth mass reflects the energetic constraints of gestation in a temperate-zone ground squirrel, where females must balance the costs of pregnancy with the need to emerge from hibernation in good condition. The brevity of the gestational phase is compensated by an extended period of lactation during which the young undergo considerable somatic growth before they are able to forage independently.

Following parturition, the neonatal mammals enter a prolonged phase of lactation dependency. The suckling juvenile stage culminates in weaning, which in this species occurs at 49 days [tx = 49 days] when measured at the same thermal regime of 35.6 °C [T = 35.6 °C]. This 7-week interval of nursing is typical for sciurids of this body size and allows the altricial pups to more than quadruple their birth mass before they begin to consume solid foods. The timing of weaning is critical, as it marks the point at which the offspring transition from a milk-based diet to the herbivorous and granivorous foods that characterize adult foraging. After weaning, the juveniles enter a sub-adult phase during which they must learn to locate food caches and avoid predators while continuing to grow. This post-weaning period is one of elevated mortality risk, as the inexperienced young are vulnerable to predation and must build body condition before their first winter.

Puberty, defined as the attainment of full gonadal maturity, is reached 365 days after birth [tp = 365 days after birth] under the same thermal conditions (35.6 °C [T = 35.6 °C]) that characterize the species' active season. This one-year interval to sexual maturation means that most individuals born in the spring will not reproduce until the following spring, effectively limiting recruitment to an annual cycle. The relatively late age at puberty, compared to smaller-bodied rodents, reflects the investment in body size required to survive hibernation and compete for breeding territories in a saturated landscape. Females that emerge from their first hibernation at lower body masses often delay reproduction further, suggesting a plastic response to environmental conditions. The pubertal threshold is closely tied to the attainment of an adult body mass that supports both the metabolic demands of gestation and the subsequent lactation period.

Adult females achieve an ultimate wet weight of 600 grams [Wwi = 600 grams], although individuals range from approximately 280 grams to 738 grams depending on habitat quality and seasonal food availability. This substantial body mass supports a relatively high basal metabolic rate; measurements conducted at 35.6 °C [T = 35.6 °C] indicate a resting oxygen consumption of 217.2 milliliters per hour [JOi = 217.2 milliliters per hour]. Such a metabolic rate is consistent with the energetic requirements of a diurnal, active forager that must maintain body temperature above ambient levels during the cool mornings of the California spring. The large body size of females likely evolved to accommodate the energetic demands of producing two litters per year, a strategy that requires considerable foraging effort during the active season. Field records show that body mass fluctuates seasonally, with individuals at their heaviest just prior to hibernation and at their lightest following emergence in late winter.

Reproductive output in this species is achieved through two distinct components: each litter contains 5 to 11 pups [N_R_i = each litter contains 5 to 11 pups], and females typically produce 2 litters each year [F_R_i = 2 litters each year], yielding a maximum annual reproductive rate of about 10 to 22 pups per female [Ri = annual reproductive rate of about 10 to 22 pups per female]. This dual-litter strategy, occurring at a body temperature of 35.6 °C [T = 35.6 °C], is unusual among temperate sciurids and likely depends on a long active season with abundant food resources. The longevity of this species is notable, with the maximum lifespan recorded at 10 years [am = 10 years] in the wild, which is also measured at 35.6 °C [T = 35.6 °C]. This extended lifespan reflects a slow life-history pace compared to smaller rodents, allowing individuals multiple breeding seasons to compensate for periodic reproductive failures. The combination of high annual fecundity with long adult survival underpins a population dynamics strategy that is resilient to the environmental stochasticity typical of California's Mediterranean climate.
